title: When does history restore what a snapshot loses?
summary: A short history makes some coarse views of Rule 110 much easier to predict. Changing the observation changes the result—and the proposed Class IV shortcut fails.
takeaway: What looks unpredictable in a snapshot can become predictable when we restore part of its path.

title: A zero commutator does not imply a linear rule
summary: Rules 4 and 200 are nonlinear, yet their commutators vanish. The earlier theorem needs a one-way implication, and the Concepts explanation has been corrected.
takeaway: A useful test can have exceptions. Preserving the counterexample is part of improving the explanation.

title: Are we predicting the background, or the moving structures?
summary: The original plan for separating background and disturbance errors, now linked to its completed frozen-protocol experiment.
takeaway: The regional test is complete; its results and remaining structural questions have their own note.

title: History helps around disturbances, too
summary: A frozen regional test finds that history improves prediction around ether departures as well as background. Most remaining errors still lie near departures.
takeaway: A path restores useful predictive context around disturbances, but a local detector does not tell us whether the predictor understands gliders.

promotion.idea: A path helps at disturbances, too

title: History and possibility: the wider research program
summary: How inherited structure enables further activity, when it becomes difficult to revise, and how to study capabilities alongside prediction.
takeaway: History matters through what it makes possible, including the ability to change the operations available next.

title: Operation order changes outcomes and how to reach them
summary: Exact enumeration separates prepared-state differences, reachable outcomes, and action responses. Equal numbers can hide different options; equal sets can hide different ways to act.
takeaway: Possibility needs an action vocabulary and a time budget. Count the options, identify them, and check how they are reached.

title: When does a useful shortcut become a constraint?
summary: The original plan now has a completed cost comparison and an all-width equivalence audit. Learning and discovery of primitives remain open.
takeaway: A bounded resource model is complete; the broader question of learning and revising useful constructions continues.

title: When does keeping a construction revisable pay?
summary: A costed comparison finds a narrow revision advantage for nearby changes. Preserving an editable trace can also cost more than replacing the construction.
takeaway: A reusable form can save coordination work while its revisability has an upfront cost. The result depends on which resources we count.

title: Does the shortcut survive a larger world?
summary: An exact causal-window audit catches a six-cell shortcut that fails elsewhere, then repeats the cost comparison with programs valid at every ring width.
takeaway: A construction can work perfectly in a small world and fail when that world expands. Verify the scope of an equivalence before reusing it.

promotion.idea: A shortcut can depend on the size of its world

title: When an earlier task returns
summary: A locally cheaper revision can cost more when an old task returns. Repeated changes can also repay the retained trace, and immediate ties can conceal different future costs.
takeaway: Available revision options, the policy for using them, and the sequence of future tasks jointly determine what a construction costs.

title: When the same bits are both a state and a rule
summary: Eight surrounding cells can encode a rule for their center. Exhaustive checks reveal a precise family of nonlinear rules whose dynamics depend on the spatial assignment.
takeaway: A shared substrate is possible; the mapping between instructions and space is part of the dynamics.

promotion.idea: A neighborhood that reads itself as an instruction

title: A dimensional rule encoding and its symmetry
summary: Outer-totalistic rules fit into the next dimension, and the resulting interpreter has a complement/reflection symmetry. Recursive closure and the proposed Class-IV connection remain open.
takeaway: A shared encoding can preserve a symmetry while its treatment of changes introduces a precise mismatch.

title: Same spacetime, different possibilities
summary: Different rules can produce the same observed path while responding differently to a perturbation. Exact enumeration separates rule identity, natural continuation, and action responses.
takeaway: A picture can predict its next steps while concealing differences that matter when we act on it.

promotion.idea: The same past can hide different responses

title: When an encoding survives evolution
summary: A fixed 2D law supports exact lower-dimensional dynamics. The search separates loss of an encoding from growth of its effective neighborhood; a conveyor construction works across dimensions.
takeaway: Preserving a representation, preserving a chosen rule neighborhood, and repairing damage are different requirements.

title: One 2D process, three exact 1D readouts
summary: Six-cell blocks implement Rule 90 under the fixed 2D interpreter. The same physical process reads as Rules 60 and 102 in moving frames; every bounded search outcome passes an independent audit.
takeaway: Encoding, frame, and cadence can change the effective law while preserving exact relationships between descriptions.

promotion.idea: One physical process, several exact descriptions

title: What happens outside the Rule-90 encoding?
summary: Exhaustive perturbations separate exact logical actions from damage to their encoding. Coordinated flips have a simple response that their individual parts do not.
takeaway: An exact encoded law depends on its action map; neighboring physical states need not repair themselves.

title: Outside one code, exact under another
summary: Longer defect runs reveal an exact Rule-90 encoding confined to two rows. It permits finite logical actions while remaining outside the original repeated code.
takeaway: Leaving one representation need not destroy organized dynamics; sparse activity alone does not demonstrate reassembly.

promotion.idea: Outside one description, exact under another

title: When exact strips meet
summary: One background row preserves independent Rule-90 strips. Direct adjacency creates nonlinear cross-influence but usually leaves the declared logical code.
takeaway: Physical interaction and composition that preserves a logical representation are different requirements.

title: The interface does not stay put
kind: Exact closure test and escape proof
summary: Keeping six bits captures one interaction step but fails on reachable states. A four-cell pulse pair provably escapes every fixed-height band.
takeaway: A description of interacting strips may need to represent growing spatial support, even when each strip alone stays confined.

title: What does pulse position actually control?
summary: Every single-bit adjacent-strip encounter launches persistent outward boundary fronts. Displacement controls an exact arithmetic delay and front signature, confirmed on a fresh range and reduced to finite contact templates.
takeaway: For this pulse family, geometry changes the scattering signature rather than the qualitative fate; pulse shape is the next control parameter.

promotion.idea: Exact boundary channels can emerge from a growing interaction wake
